note: Self-correcting out loud is disarming and buys forgiveness.

text: Mình sẽ gửi biên bản sau.
sample: I'll send round the notes afterwards.
note: Distribute to a group. Standard British office usage.

text: Mình nghĩ ta cần một buổi riêng cho việc này.
sample: This probably needs its own meeting.
note: Recognising scope openly saves an hour of drift.

text: Cảm ơn mọi người đã dành thời gian.
sample: Thanks, everyone — useful session.
note: Two-word sign-off that closes a call warmly.

text: Mình xin phép rời sớm mười phút.
sample: I'll have to drop off a bit early.
note: Leaving a call. Say it at the start, not as you vanish.

text: Chúng ta quyết luôn được không?
sample: Can we make a call on this today?
note: Pushes for a decision. The phrase that ends circular meetings.

text: Mình cần làm rõ một điểm.
sample: Just to be clear on one thing —
note: Prefaces a correction politely. Very high-frequency.

text: Mình sẽ nói ngắn thôi.
sample: I'll be brief.
note: Two words. Then actually be brief, or you lose the room.

text: Mọi người có bổ sung gì không?
sample: Anything I’ve missed?
note: Invites correction while showing you already did the work.

text: Open a fifteen-minute demo of a feature nobody has seen. Three sentences.
sample: Quick context: this is the export flow people kept complaining about. I'll show it working, then the one thing that's still rough. Hold questions till the end if you can.
note: Context, promise, ground rules. Every good demo starts here.

text: Interrupt a colleague who has been talking for ten minutes, politely.
sample: Sorry to cut across you — can I check something before we go further?
note: Apologise, name the act, give a reason. Interruption made acceptable.

text: You are asked a question you cannot answer in front of fifteen people. Handle it in two sentences.
sample: I don't want to guess at that in front of everyone. Let me get you the actual number by this afternoon.
chunk: I don't want to guess at that
note: Refusing to bluff reads as competence, not weakness.

text: Two people are arguing in your meeting and time is running out. Intervene.
sample: You two clearly need twenty minutes on this, and it isn't now. Can you take it away and come back with a recommendation?
note: Ends a debate by assigning it as homework.

text: Your screen share is frozen and everyone is waiting. Fill the silence.
sample: Bear with me — while that sorts itself out, the short version is that load times dropped by half.
note: Buys time gracefully and keeps delivering value meanwhile.

text: Present bad news to stakeholders: the project will slip by three weeks. Three sentences.
sample: We're going to be three weeks late, and I'd rather tell you now than at the deadline. The cause was the migration, not the team. Here's what I'm changing so it doesn't happen twice.
chunk: I'd rather tell you now than ___
note: Owns the delay, explains, then pivots to action.

text: Someone repeats a point you made earlier as if it were theirs. Reclaim it without friction.
sample: Yes — that's exactly the point I was making earlier, so it sounds like we agree.
chunk: that's exactly the point I was making
note: Reclaims credit while appearing generous. Very effective.

text: Wrap up a meeting that has achieved nothing, in three sentences.
sample: Right — we haven't landed this, so let's not pretend we have. I'll write up the two options and we'll decide by Thursday on email. Thanks all.
note: Honesty plus a plan. Far better than a vague “great chat”.

text: Ask a silent colleague for their view without putting them on the spot.
sample: Linh, you've been closest to this — anything we're missing, even half-formed?
note: Lowers the bar so a quiet person can speak safely.

text: Disagree with your manager in front of the team, respectfully.
sample: I see it differently, and I might be wrong. My worry is we're optimising the bit users don't touch. Happy to be talked out of it.
chunk: happy to be talked out of it
note: Stakes a position while staying genuinely open. Disarms hierarchy.

text: Introduce yourself in a meeting with a new client. Two sentences.
sample: I'm Jane, I look after the backend side of this. If something breaks at two in the morning, I'm the one who gets the call.
chunk: I'm the one who gets the call
note: Memorable self-introduction. Concrete beats job titles.

text: Handle a hostile question at the end of your presentation.
sample: That's a fair challenge. You're right that the sample was small — here's why I still think the direction holds.
note: Concedes the valid part first. Removes all the heat.

text: Chair a meeting back on track after ten minutes of tangent.
sample: We've drifted a fair way from the agenda — can we park the pricing chat and finish the launch date?
note: Parks without killing. The chair’s most useful phrase.

text: Explain a technical problem to a non-technical audience in three sentences.
sample: Think of it like a motorway with one lane closed. Everything still gets through, just slowly, and at rush hour it stops entirely. We're reopening the lane, which takes about two weeks.
note: Analogy first, detail second. Non-technical rooms follow this easily.

text: Volunteer for an action item and set expectations in two sentences.
sample: I'll take that one. Realistically it'll be Wednesday rather than Monday — shout if that's a problem.
note: Commits, sets a real date, invites objection. Fully professional.

text: Cho mình hỏi đây có phải phòng khám không ạ?
sample: Hello, is that the surgery?
note: On the phone, use “that” for the other end. Never “is this”.

text: Mình gọi về cái đơn hàng tuần trước.
sample: I'm calling about an order I placed last week.
note: State your business in sentence one. Saves five minutes.

text: Mình chờ được, không sao.
sample: That's fine, I'll hold.
note: The phone-queue phrase. Two words, endlessly needed.

text: Cho mình nói với người phụ trách được không?
sample: Could I speak to whoever handles billing?
note: Gets you past the wrong person without knowing any names.

text: Mình bị chuyển máy ba lần rồi.
sample: I've been transferred three times already.
note: Passive plus a count. Applies pressure without any rudeness.

text: Mình xin số tham chiếu ạ.
sample: Could I take a reference number for this?
note: Always ask. It makes the next call ten times easier.

text: Mình đã gửi giấy tờ tuần trước rồi.
sample: I sent the documents over last Tuesday.
note: “Over” adds the sense of delivery to another party.

text: Mình cần gia hạn hộ chiếu.
sample: I need to renew my passport.
note: Renew a passport, a visa, a subscription, a licence.

text: Mình muốn đổi lịch hẹn.
sample: I need to rearrange an appointment.
note: Rearrange = move to another time. Cancel means don’t rebook.

text: Mình chưa nhận được thư nào cả.
sample: I haven't had anything through yet.
note: Post, emails and payments all “come through”. Very idiomatic.

text: Mình cần xác nhận bằng email.
sample: Could you confirm that in writing?
note: The three words that protect you in any dispute.

text: Bạn nhắc lại giúp mình chậm hơn được không?
sample: Sorry, could you say that a bit slower?
note: Never pretend you caught a number. Always ask.

text: Mình đánh vần tên cho bạn.
sample: I'll spell it for you.
note: Offer before they ask. Saves the whole exchange.

text: Mình muốn khiếu nại.
sample: I'd like to make a complaint.
note: The formal trigger phrase. It changes how you are handled.

text: Chuyện này bao giờ giải quyết xong ạ?
sample: What's the timeframe on this?
note: Asks for a date without sounding aggressive.

text: Mình cần nói chuyện với cấp trên của bạn.
sample: Could you put me through to your manager?
note: Put through = connect a call. The escalation phrase.

text: Mình đã trả tiền rồi mà vẫn bị nhắc.
sample: I've already paid and I'm still getting reminders.
note: Present continuous for an ongoing annoyance. Very clear.

text: Mình muốn huỷ dịch vụ này.
sample: I'd like to cancel my account, please.
note: Say it plainly. Hedging invites a retention script.

text: Mình mất giấy tờ đó rồi.
sample: I've lost the paperwork, I'm afraid.
note: Softens bad news about yourself. Very British, very useful.

text: Mình cần cái đó gấp.
sample: It's fairly urgent, if possible.
note: Understated urgency works better than shouting on the phone.

text: Bạn có thể gửi lại cho mình không?
sample: Could you send it through again?
note: Through = via a channel. Email, post, portal, anything.

text: Mình sẽ gọi lại sau ạ.
sample: I'll try again later, thanks.
note: Ends a dead-end call politely and keeps the door open.

text: Tên mình là Jane, J-A-N-E.
sample: It's Jane — that's J for Juliet, A for Alpha.
note: Spelling with words, not letters. The only reliable method on a phone line.

text: Mình cần chứng minh địa chỉ.
sample: They want proof of address.
note: Proof of address, of income, of identity. The bureaucratic trio.

text: Giấy này cần công chứng không ạ?
sample: Does this need to be certified?
note: Certified = officially verified. Ask before you queue.

text: Mình đã đặt lịch trực tuyến rồi.
sample: I booked it online, under Jane Pham.
note: Past simple plus your name. Everything they need at once.

text: Mình muốn biết tình trạng đơn của mình.
sample: I'm just chasing an application I submitted in June.
note: Chase = politely pursue a slow response. Hugely useful at work too.

text: Mình cần hoá đơn có tên công ty.
sample: Could I get an invoice with the company name on it?
note: Specifies a requirement casually. Sounds far more natural than a clause.

text: Mình đã chờ hai mươi phút rồi.
sample: I've been on hold for twenty minutes.
note: Fixed phrase. Never “in hold” or “waiting the line”.

text: Mình sẽ đợi thư của bạn.
sample: I'll wait to hear from you.
note: Ends a call by handing them the next action.

text: Cảm ơn bạn đã giúp ạ.
sample: You've been really helpful, thank you.
note: Say it when it is true. Phone staff remember it.

text: Call your bank about a charge you do not recognise. Three sentences.
sample: There's a charge on my account from the 14th I don't recognise — forty pounds, something called NXT Ltd. I haven't authorised anything like that. Can you tell me what it is and freeze the card if not?
note: Facts, denial, two clear requests. The template for every bank call.

text: You have been on hold for twenty-five minutes and someone finally answers. Open the call.
sample: Hi — I've been holding a while, so I'll be quick. It's about a refund from the 3rd, reference 88412.
note: Mentions the wait once, then gets straight to it. Wins them over.

text: Cancel a subscription while the agent pushes a discount. Hold the line in three sentences.
sample: I appreciate the offer, but I've made the decision. I'd just like it cancelled today, please. Could you email me confirmation?
note: Closed sentence with no opening for a counter-offer.

text: Explain to a landlord over the phone that the boiler has failed. Two sentences.
sample: The boiler's stopped completely — no heating and no hot water since last night. What's the soonest someone can come out?
note: For tradespeople visiting. “Come out” is the standard phrasal verb.

text: A delivery has gone to the wrong address. Sort it out on a call.
sample: The tracking says delivered, but nothing's arrived here. Can you check the address it actually went to, and resend or refund?
note: Cites their own evidence. Very hard to argue with.

text: Ring a clinic to book an appointment for a specific date and time.
sample: Morning — I'd like to book an appointment, ideally Thursday afternoon. Any time after two works for me.
chunk: any time after ___ works for me
note: Gives a window rather than a single slot. Gets booked faster.

text: Chase a slow visa application politely, by phone.
sample: I'm just chasing an application from the 2nd of June, reference VS4419. It's past the stated processing time — is there anything I can do from my end?
note: Offers to help rather than complain. Often unlocks real information.

text: Dispute a parking fine over the phone, in three sentences.
sample: I've had a fine for the 12th, but I had a valid ticket that day and I've still got it. I'd like to appeal. What do you need from me?
chunk: what do you need from me
note: Skips the argument and moves straight to the process.

text: You reach an automated menu with no option matching your problem. Explain to the human at the end.
sample: None of the menu options really covered it, so I've ended up with you — hopefully you can point me the right way.
note: Apologetic and disarming. The human almost always helps.

text: Leave a voicemail asking for a callback. Three sentences.
sample: Hi, it's Jane Pham, calling about invoice 2214. Best number is 0790 double-two, three-one. Any time before six is fine — thanks.
note: Name, reason, number, window. The complete voicemail formula.

text: Report a lost bank card over the phone, urgently.
sample: I need to report a card lost, straight away please. Last transaction I made was a coffee this morning — anything after that isn't me.
note: Draws a clear line for the fraud team. Extremely practical.

text: A company insists you already signed something you did not. Push back on the call.
sample: I haven't signed anything to that effect, and I'd like to see whatever you're looking at. Can you email me a copy today?
note: Formal, precise, and slightly legal. Changes the tone of the call.

text: Ask an official what documents you need to bring, and write them down as they speak.
sample: Let me write this down — passport, proof of address, and the original certificate. Anything else, or is that the lot?
note: Confirms completeness in four words. Prevents a second trip.

text: You need to correct a misspelling of your name on an official record.
sample: My surname's been recorded as Phan rather than Pham — P-H-A-M. What's the process for getting that corrected?
note: Asks about the system rather than blaming the person. Gets results.

text: Close a long, frustrating call on a positive note.
sample: Look, I know none of this was your doing — thanks for actually sorting it. Have a good afternoon.
chunk: none of this was your doing
note: Separates the person from the institution. They will remember you.

text: Cho mình gọi món này nhé.
sample: I'll have the beef pho, please.
note: The ordering formula. Present simple “I have” would sound wrong.

text: Cho mình xem menu ạ.
sample: Could we see the menu, please?
note: “Could we” for a table, “could I” alone. Small but noticed.

text: Món này có gì trong đó ạ?
sample: What's in this one?
note: Four words that prevent every allergy disaster.

text: Món nào ngon nhất ở đây ạ?
sample: What's good here?
note: Trusts the staff. Almost always gets you the best dish.

text: Mình không ăn được đồ cay.
sample: I can't really handle spicy food.
note: Handle = tolerate. Sounds like a preference, not a complaint.

text: Cho mình ít cay thôi nhé.
sample: Could you go easy on the chilli?
note: Go easy on = use less. Works for salt, ice, garlic, everything.

text: Mình ăn chay.
sample: I'm vegetarian.
note: No article. “I am a vegetarian” is correct but sounds formal.

text: Mình dị ứng đậu phộng.
sample: I've got a peanut allergy.
note: Stronger and clearer than “I don’t eat peanuts”. Use this one.

text: Cho mình thêm một bát nữa.
sample: Could we get another bowl?
note: “Another” already means one more. Don’t add “one more”.

text: Món này ngon quá.
sample: This is really good.
note: Simple and sincere. Over-describing food sounds odd in English.

text: Mình no rồi.
sample: I'm stuffed.
note: Cheerfully very full. The most-used word at the end of a meal.

text: Mình ăn không hết.
sample: I can't finish this.
note: No shame in it. Follow with “could I take it away?”

text: Cho mình gói mang về ạ.
sample: Could we get this to take away?
note: British; Americans say “to go”. Both are understood anywhere.

text: Món này hơi mặn.
sample: It's a bit on the salty side.
note: Softens any criticism of food. Very diplomatic.

text: Món của mình chưa ra.
sample: I think my order got missed.
note: Passive with “got”. Blames the process, not the waiter.

text: Mình gọi món khác cơ.
sample: I actually ordered the chicken.
note: “Actually” marks the correction gently. Essential word here.

text: Cho mình tính tiền nhé.
sample: Could we have the bill, please?
note: British. Americans say “the check”. Don’t say “the money”.

text: Quán này đông lắm, phải đặt trước.
sample: You need to book — it gets packed.
note: “Packed” for crowded places. Short, vivid, current.

text: Mình muốn đặt bàn cho bốn người.
sample: I'd like to book a table for four, please.
note: The fixed reservation phrase. Number only, no “people”.

text: Mình đói lắm rồi.
sample: I'm starving.
note: Hyperbole, but standard. “I have hunger” does not exist.

text: Mình ăn sáng ở nhà rồi.
sample: I've already eaten, thanks.
note: Present perfect for the recent past. Declines food politely.

text: Món này ăn kèm với gì ạ?
sample: What does it come with?
note: Asks about sides. Prevents ordering rice twice.

text: Cho mình nước lọc thôi ạ.
sample: Just tap water for me, thanks.
note: The free option, named without embarrassment.

text: Mình thử một miếng được không?
sample: Can I try a bit?
note: Sharing food, stated casually. Very natural among friends.

text: Mình tự nấu cho tiết kiệm.
sample: I've been cooking more to save money.
note: Comparative adverb. Implies a change of habit.

text: Mình nấu dở lắm.
sample: I'm a terrible cook.
note: Self-deprecating and completely idiomatic. Always gets a laugh.

text: Cái này để lâu chưa chắc còn ăn được.
sample: I think this has gone off.
note: Gone off = spoiled. Milk, meat, and occasionally people.

text: Mình đặt đồ ăn giao đến nhé.
sample: Shall we just get a delivery?
note: The modern default. “Order in” also works perfectly.

text: Quán này giá phải chăng.
sample: It's pretty reasonable, actually.
note: Reasonable = fairly priced. Never say “cheap” about a restaurant you like.

text: Mình không thích rau mùi.
sample: I can't stand coriander.
note: Strong dislike, stated lightly. Extremely common with coriander.

text: Ăn xong mình buồn ngủ quá.
sample: That's sent me straight to sleep.
note: Food as the agent. Vivid and very natural.

text: Mình ăn ngoài nhiều quá.
sample: I've been eating out far too much.
note: Eat out = eat at restaurants. Not “eat outside”.

text: Món này mẹ mình nấu ngon hơn.
sample: My mum does a better version, honestly.
note: Warm and slightly boastful. Works for any family dish.

text: Mình để dành phần cho bạn.
sample: I've saved you some.
note: Small kindness, perfectly phrased. Learn it exactly.

text: Bữa này mình mời.
sample: Put your wallet away.
note: Claims the bill without mentioning money at all. Warm and very natural.

text: Order for the table at a restaurant where nobody can decide. Three sentences.
sample: Shall I just order a few things to share? I'll get the pho, the spring rolls and the grilled pork — shout if you want anything else.
note: Takes charge without overruling anyone. Everybody is relieved.

text: Explain your dietary requirement to a waiter who seems unsure. Two sentences.
sample: I've got a peanut allergy, so I have to be a bit annoying about it. Could you check with the kitchen whether the sauce has any in?
note: Pre-apologising makes staff take it seriously rather than resent it.

text: Recommend your favourite local dish to a visitor — three sentences.
sample: You have to try bun cha. It's grilled pork in a broth you dip noodles into, and it sounds wrong until you eat it. Go at lunch, never dinner.
chunk: it sounds wrong until you eat it
note: Handles the scepticism before the listener raises it.

text: Decline a second helping without offending your host.
sample: It was genuinely lovely — I couldn't manage another bite, though.
note: Praise first, refusal second. The order matters enormously.

text: The bill has an item you did not order. Raise it with the waiter.
sample: Sorry, could we check the bill? I don't think we had the second bottle.
note: Hedged, polite, and impossible to take badly.

text: You are cooking for a friend and burn the main dish. Improvise out loud.
sample: Right — that's not happening. Give me ten minutes and we're having very good eggs instead.
note: Announces failure with confidence. Far funnier than apologising.

text: Split a shared dinner order fairly with two friends over the bill.
sample: Easiest thing is just thirds — we all had a bit of everything. Anyone unhappy with that?
note: Proposes the simplest fair method and invites objection.

text: Tell a friend you cannot eat at the place they chose, and suggest another.
sample: I'd be eating chips all night at that one — any chance we do the Vietnamese place instead?
note: Explains the problem with a joke. Nobody feels criticised.

text: A waiter asks how everything was, and it was mediocre. Answer honestly but kindly.
sample: The starter was lovely. The main was a bit much for me, honestly — but no complaints about the service.
note: Honest, specific, and generous where it can be.

text: Teach someone to make your simplest home dish in three sentences.
sample: Fry the garlic until it just turns gold, not brown. Add the greens and a splash of fish sauce, thirty seconds, no more. That's it — anything else and you've ruined it.
note: Ends with the warning. The most memorable part of any recipe.

text: You have been waiting fifty minutes for food. Ask about it without being rude.
sample: Sorry to chase — any idea how far off our food is? We're not in a rush, just wondering.
note: Asks for information, not an apology. Always works better.

text: Explain to a visitor why breakfast in your country is different — three sentences.
sample: Breakfast here is a proper meal, usually soup or rice, eaten standing up on a plastic stool. Nobody has cereal. You'll be full by seven and hungry again by eleven.
note: Blunt contrast. Funnier and clearer than any explanation.

text: Mình có một anh trai và một em gái.
sample: I've got an older brother and a younger sister.
note: English has no built-in age words. You must add older or younger.

text: Bố mẹ mình sống ở Hà Nội.
sample: My parents are based in Hanoi.
note: Based in = live and work there. Slightly more adult than “live”.

text: Mình là con một.
sample: I'm an only child.
note: Fixed phrase. Never “I am the only son” unless that is the point.

text: Mình giống mẹ hơn.
sample: I take after my mum.
note: Take after = resemble in looks or character. Family-specific verb.

text: Mình đã cưới rồi.
sample: I'm married.
note: State, not event. “I married” needs an object to make sense.

text: Mình có bạn gái ba năm rồi.
sample: I've been with my girlfriend for three years.
note: “Been with” for relationships. Present perfect, always.

text: Bọn mình chia tay rồi.
sample: We split up a few months ago.
note: Split up = break up. Neutral, and easier to say.

text: Mình vừa lên chức chú.
sample: I've just become an uncle.
note: Present perfect for news. Announce it exactly like this.

text: Mình về nhà mỗi Tết.
sample: I go home every Tet.
note: No preposition. “Go to home” is the classic mistake.

text: Mình nhớ bố mẹ.
sample: I miss my parents.
note: Miss takes a direct object. No “miss to” or “miss about”.

text: Bố mình nghiêm lắm.
sample: My dad was pretty strict with us.
note: Strict with people, strict about rules. Two prepositions.

text: Mẹ mình gọi mình mỗi ngày.
sample: My mum rings me every single day.
note: Ring = phone, in British English. Warmer than “calls”.

text: Nhà mình đông người.
sample: We were a big household.
note: Household = everyone under one roof. Fits Vietnamese families well.

text: Mình lớn lên ở quê.
sample: I grew up in the countryside.
note: Grow up = spend your childhood. Not “raised up”.

text: Vợ mình làm giáo viên.
sample: My wife teaches primary school.
note: Jobs as verbs when possible. Sounds more natural than “is a teacher”.

text: Bọn mình sắp có em bé.
sample: We're expecting.
note: One word, complete announcement. Everyone understands it.

text: Con mình hai tuổi.
sample: My son's two.
note: Age with no noun. Adding “years old” here sounds heavy.

text: Mình chăm bố mẹ già.
sample: I look after my parents now.
note: Look after = care for. The right verb for family duty.

text: Bọn mình họp gia đình mỗi Chủ nhật.
sample: The whole family gets together on Sundays.
note: Get together = meet socially. The noun is “a get-together”.

text: Mình cãi nhau với em trai.
sample: I had a row with my brother.
note: Row rhymes with “now”. Very British word for an argument.

text: Bọn mình đã làm hoà.
sample: We've made up since.
note: Make up = reconcile. “Since” carries the whole story.

text: Mình giống bố ở tính cách.
sample: I'm my father's son, for better or worse.
note: Ironic self-awareness. A very English way to admit heredity.

text: Mình sống một mình từ mười tám tuổi.
sample: I've lived on my own since I was eighteen.
note: On my own = alone, by choice. Warmer than “alone”.

text: Mình là cháu lớn nhất.
sample: I'm the eldest of the grandchildren.
note: Eldest for people, oldest for things. British distinction.

text: Anh ấy là bạn thân từ nhỏ.
sample: We've been mates since we were seven.
note: British for close friends. Extremely common and warm.

text: Mình coi bạn ấy như em ruột.
sample: She's basically a sister to me.
note: Upgrades a friendship to family. Very affectionate.

text: Mình sắp cưới tháng sau.
sample: I'm getting married next month.
note: Present continuous for a fixed plan. Never “I will marry”.

text: Bố mẹ mình ly hôn từ lúc mình nhỏ.
sample: My parents divorced when I was small.
note: Small = young, for children. Common and gentle.

text: Mình ít nói chuyện với họ hàng.
sample: I'm not that close to the extended family.
note: Aunts, uncles, cousins. One phrase covers all of them.

text: Anh mình nuôi mình ăn học.
sample: My brother put me through university.
note: Paid for your education. Enormously respectful phrasing.

text: Mình biết ơn bố mẹ nhiều.
sample: I owe my parents more than I can say.
note: Gratitude that admits its own limits. Very moving.

text: Bọn mình vẫn giữ liên lạc.
sample: We're still in touch.
note: Keep in touch, stay in touch, get in touch. Learn all three.

text: Phone home after three months of silence. Open the call in three sentences.
sample: Hi Mum — I know, it's been ages, I'm sorry. Work ate the whole spring. Tell me everything, starting with Dad's knee.
note: Apologise briefly, then hand them the floor. Very disarming.

text: Introduce your partner to your parents for the first time.
sample: Mum, Dad — this is Linh. She's heard a frankly unreasonable amount about both of you.
note: Light joke that warms the room instantly.

text: Tell your parents you are moving abroad. Three sentences.
sample: I've been offered something in Berlin, and I'm going to take it. It's two years, not forever, and I'll be back for Tet every year. I need you to be pleased for me, even if you're not yet.
note: Asks for support honestly. Acknowledges their feelings without waiting.

text: Decline a family wedding you cannot attend, to your aunt, kindly.
sample: I'm so sorry — I genuinely can't get there for the 14th. I'll ring them on the day, and I'd love to see the photos.
note: “Genuinely” does the work that a long excuse would do badly.

text: A relative asks when you are getting married. Deflect warmly.
sample: You'll be the second to know, I promise. How's your garden this year?
chunk: you'll be the second to know
note: Charming non-answer plus a change of subject. Works every time.

text: Apologise to your sibling for something from years ago. Three sentences.
sample: I've been meaning to say this for about ten years: I was horrible to you the summer you moved. I was jealous, which isn't an excuse. I'm sorry, properly.
chunk: I've been meaning to say this for ___
note: Names the delay. Makes the apology land as genuine.

text: Ask your parents about their life before you were born.
sample: What were you actually like at my age? Not the version you tell at dinner — the real one.
chunk: not the version you tell at ___
note: Asks for honesty playfully. Often unlocks real stories.

text: Explain your family to a foreign colleague in three sentences.
sample: There are four of us, and somehow eleven people at every meal. My grandmother lives with us, which is normal here and apparently not in Sweden. Nobody knocks.
note: One concrete detail beats three sentences of explanation.

text: Console a friend whose relationship just ended, in three sentences.
sample: You don't have to be okay about it yet. Come over, bring nothing, we'll order too much food. You can tell me the whole thing twice if you want.
note: Removes every obstacle to accepting comfort.

text: Set a boundary with a parent who keeps commenting on your job.
sample: I know it comes from worry, and I need you to stop asking about it every call. Ask me about anything else and I'll talk for an hour.
note: Names their good intention before refusing the behaviour.

text: Tell a close friend you are proud of them, in two sentences.
sample: I've watched you build that from nothing while everyone told you not to. I don't say it enough, but I'm quietly proud of you.
note: Admitting the gap makes the compliment more credible.

text: Describe your grandmother in three sentences, without adjectives like nice.
sample: She's four foot eleven and rules the house from a plastic chair. She has fed everyone who has ever walked through the door, including the postman. She thinks I'm too thin, which she has thought since 1996.
note: A specific date makes a portrait funny and real.

text: Ask a friend for a big favour — looking after your flat for a month.
sample: This is a proper ask, so say no freely: could you keep an eye on the flat in August? Water the plants, nothing else, and I'll bring you something good back.
note: Giving explicit permission to refuse makes people more likely to accept.

text: Reconnect with an old friend after years apart. Write the first message.
sample: This is going to be out of nowhere, but I walked past our old place today and thought of you. How are you? Genuinely, how are you?
note: Explains the randomness, which makes it charming rather than odd.

text: Tell your family about a decision they will not like, at dinner. Three sentences.
sample: I want to tell you all together rather than one at a time: I'm leaving the company. I've thought about it for months and I'm not asking permission. I am asking you to trust me on it.
note: Clear, respectful, and impossible to misread.

text: Mình học được hai năm rồi.
sample: I've been learning for about two years.
note: Present perfect continuous. The tense for an unfinished effort.

text: Bạn giải thích lại giúp mình nhé.
sample: Could you explain that another way?
note: Asks for a different angle, not a repetition. Much more useful.

text: Mình học kiểu tự học.
sample: I'm mostly self-taught.
note: One hyphenated word. A quiet point of pride in tech.

text: Mình hay quên từ vựng.
sample: Vocabulary just doesn't stick for me.
note: Stick = stay in memory. The exact verb learners need.

text: Mình luyện nói mỗi tối mười lăm phút.
sample: I do fifteen minutes of speaking practice every evening.
note: Noun + noun. Simpler than “practice of speaking”.

text: Mình nghe hiểu tốt hơn nói.
sample: My listening is way ahead of my speaking.
note: “Way” intensifies the gap. Very natural and current.

text: Mình sợ nói sai.
sample: I'm scared of making mistakes out loud.
note: Names the real fear precisely. Most learners recognise it.

text: Mình cần luyện phát âm.
sample: I need to work on my pronunciation.
note: Note the spelling — no “pronounciation”. Very common error.

text: Mình bị kẹt ở trình độ này lâu rồi.
sample: I've plateaued a bit.
note: Fixed metaphor for stalled progress. One word does it all.

text: Mình học theo nhóm cho có động lực.
sample: I study with a group to keep myself honest.
note: Accountability, stated with humour. Very likeable phrasing.

text: Mình bỏ dở khoá đó rồi.
sample: I never finished that one, if I’m honest.
note: Honest admission. Everyone has an abandoned course.

text: Mình học tốt nhất vào buổi sáng.
sample: I take things in best in the morning.
note: Take in = absorb information. Very common phrasal verb.

text: Mình cần ôn lại từ tuần trước.
sample: I need to go back over last week’s material.
note: Go back over = revise. Implies a second pass.

text: Mình thi tuần sau.
sample: I've got an exam next week.
note: Have got for possession. British and conversational.

text: Mình ôn thi cả đêm.
sample: I crammed the whole night before.
note: Cram = study intensively at the last minute. Universally understood.

text: Mình thi trượt môn đó.
sample: I failed that one, twice actually.
note: Plain and unashamed. Adding a number owns it completely.

text: Mình học lại từ đầu.
sample: I'm starting again from scratch.
note: From the very beginning. Fixed idiom, never “from zero”.

text: Mình học được nhiều từ việc dạy lại.
sample: I learn most when I have to explain it to someone.
note: Names your own best method. Useful and self-aware.

text: Mình mất tập trung nhanh.
sample: My concentration goes after about twenty minutes.
note: “Goes” for something that fails. Simple and idiomatic.

text: Mình ghi chép bằng tay.
sample: I take notes by hand — it sticks better.
note: Take notes, not write notes. Fixed collocation.

text: Mình đọc chậm nhưng hiểu sâu.
sample: I'm a slow reader, but it goes in properly.
note: Go in = be absorbed. Learner-friendly and very natural.

text: Mình cần phản hồi để tiến bộ.
sample: I can't improve without someone correcting me.
note: States a requirement clearly. Invites the help you need.

text: Mình học vì thích, không vì bằng.
sample: I'm doing it out of interest, not for a certificate.
note: “Out of” for motivation. Out of interest, out of habit, out of spite.

text: Mình hay so sánh mình với người khác.
sample: I compare myself to other people far too much.
note: Reflexive verb plus “to”. The grammar of self-criticism.

text: Mình tiến bộ chậm mà chắc.
sample: It's slow, but it's going in the right direction.
note: Optimism that stays honest. Very reusable.

text: Mình quên hết những gì học hồi đại học.
sample: I've forgotten nearly everything from university.
note: Present perfect for a current state of loss.

text: Mình học tiếng Anh để đi làm nước ngoài.
sample: I'm learning English to work abroad.
note: Infinitive of purpose. Simplest way to state a goal.

text: Mình luyện tập mỗi ngày một ít.
sample: A little bit every day beats three hours on Sunday.
note: The whole philosophy of practice in one line.

text: Mình hỏi thầy sau giờ học.
sample: I asked the teacher afterwards, one to one.
note: Private, individual. Also spelled one-to-one when used as an adjective.

text: Mình sẽ không bỏ lần này.
sample: I'm not quitting this time.
note: Simple, present, and said out loud. That is the point.

text: Ask a teacher to explain something again, without feeling stupid. Two sentences.
sample: Can I check I've got this right — you're saying the tense changes because of the time reference? Sorry, I'd rather ask now than guess for a week.
chunk: I'd rather ask now than guess
note: Reframes the question as efficiency, not weakness.

text: Explain your English learning routine to someone who asks. Three sentences.
sample: Fifteen minutes of speaking out loud every night, even when it's rubbish. I read one article and steal three phrases from it. The trick isn't the hours, it's not skipping days.
note: Concrete and slightly funny. Memorable as advice.

text: A friend says they want to learn to code. Give them one piece of real advice.
sample: Build something you actually want to exist, and finish it badly. Courses will keep you busy for a year and teach you less than one finished thing.
note: Counterintuitive advice, stated confidently. Lands hard.

text: You did badly on a test. Talk to your teacher about what to change.
sample: I got sixty percent and I know why — I never practised the listening section. Could you point me at what to drill for next month?
note: Owns the failure and asks for direction. Teachers respond to this.

text: Tell a native speaker you want them to correct your English.
sample: Do me a favour — correct me when I get things wrong, even mid-sentence. I promise I won't take it personally.
note: Removes their hesitation. The single most useful sentence for a learner.

text: Explain a concept you know well to someone who knows nothing about it.
sample: Think of a database as a very strict spreadsheet that refuses to let you be careless. Everything after that is just how you ask it questions.
note: Compresses a big topic into one honest simplification.

text: Ask a colleague to teach you something they are good at.
sample: You're clearly the person who understands the deployment side. Any chance of half an hour where you just talk and I take notes?
chunk: any chance of half an hour
note: Small, specific, flattering ask. Very hard to refuse.

text: Motivate a friend who wants to quit learning a language, in three sentences.
sample: You're at the bit where it stops feeling like progress, and everyone quits here. You can already do things you couldn't do in January. Give it six more weeks, then decide.
note: Names the plateau. Makes it feel normal rather than personal.

text: Tell a class you do not understand the homework, in front of everyone.
sample: Sorry — can I ask a basic question? I don't think I've understood what we're actually meant to produce.
chunk: can I ask a basic question?
note: Owning the basicness of a question makes it easy to ask.

text: Explain why you are learning English, in two sentences, without clichés.
sample: I can do my job in English on paper and not in a room. I'm fixing the gap between those two things.
note: Precise and unsentimental. Far better than “for my future”.

text: Give feedback to a teacher whose lessons are too easy for you.
sample: The lessons are really clear — I'm just not being stretched much. Could we push into harder material, even if I struggle?
note: Asks for difficulty explicitly. Rare, and teachers love it.

text: Describe your biggest weakness as a learner honestly, in two sentences.
sample: I start things enthusiastically and abandon them around week three. I've started building in a check-in so it's harder to quiet-quit on myself.
note: Self-aware and specific. Shows the fix as well as the flaw.

text: Ask someone to be your study partner and set the terms.
sample: Fancy doing this together? Twenty minutes, twice a week, and either of us can cancel without an excuse.
note: Low-commitment framing. Makes people far more likely to agree.

text: Máy mình bị treo rồi.
sample: My laptop's frozen.
note: Frozen for an unresponsive machine. Not “hanged” or “stopped”.

text: Mình khởi động lại thử xem.
sample: I'll try restarting it.
note: Restart, not “reopen”. The universal first fix.

text: Wifi nhà mình yếu quá.
sample: The wifi here is dreadful.
note: British intensifier for bad. Stronger than “not good”.

text: Mình mất mạng lúc đó.
sample: I dropped off the call for a second.
note: Standard phrasing for losing a connection mid-meeting.

text: Điện thoại mình gần hết pin.
sample: My phone's about to die.
note: Phones die. Never “my phone is finishing battery”.

text: Mình cần sạc gấp.
sample: Have you got a charger I could borrow?
note: Full polite request. Adding “I could borrow” makes it easy to say yes.

text: Mình bị mất hết dữ liệu.
sample: I've lost the lot.
note: British for lost everything. Compact and dramatic.

text: Mình có sao lưu không nhỉ?
sample: Please tell me that was backed up.
note: The two most important words in computing.

text: Mình quên mật khẩu rồi.
sample: I've forgotten my password again.

text: Mình cần cập nhật phần mềm.
sample: It needs updating.
note: Need + gerund for a passive requirement. Very British.

text: Màn hình bị nứt rồi.
sample: I've cracked the screen.
note: Crack for glass. You cracked it; it did not break itself.

text: Ứng dụng này cứ tự tắt.
sample: The app keeps crashing.
note: Keep + -ing for a recurring fault. The standard bug report.

text: Mình thử tắt đi bật lại chưa?
sample: Have you tried turning it off and on again?
chunk: turning it off and on again
note: A joke and genuine advice. Say it with a straight face.

text: Mình không nhận được thông báo.
sample: I'm not getting notifications.
note: Get, not receive. Receive sounds like a formal letter.

text: Mình cần chuyển dữ liệu sang máy mới.
sample: I need to move everything across to the new one.
note: “Across” for transferring between devices. Very natural.

text: Máy này dùng được ba năm rồi.
sample: I've had this one about three years.

text: Mình đang cân nhắc đổi máy.
sample: I'm thinking about upgrading.
note: Upgrade covers phones, laptops, plans, everything.

text: Cái này dùng dễ hơn nhiều.
sample: It's much more intuitive than the old one.
note: The exact word for easy-to-figure-out. Sounds informed.

text: Mình không hiểu cái nút này làm gì.
sample: I've no idea what that button does.
note: Honest and idiomatic. Never “I do not know this button”.

text: Mình cài lại từ đầu.
sample: I ended up doing a clean install.
note: The fixed term for wiping and starting over.

text: Mình để chế độ im lặng.
sample: I've put it on silent.
note: On silent, on mute, on airplane mode. All take “on”.

text: Mình gửi qua link cho nhanh.
sample: I'll just send you a link.
note: “Just” makes an action sound effortless and immediate.

text: Mình chưa quen dùng cái này.
sample: I'm still getting used to it.
note: Get used to = adapt. Always followed by a noun or gerund.

text: Mình tắt hết thông báo cho tập trung.
sample: I've turned everything off to get some peace.
note: The reason, stated humanly. Better than “to focus”.

text: Camera mình không bật được.
sample: My camera won’t come on.
note: Won’t = refuses to. Perfect for stubborn devices.

text: Mình bị lỗi khi thanh toán.
sample: It threw an error when I tried to pay.
note: Developer phrasing, now widely used. Precise and confident.

text: Mình cần hai bước xác thực.
sample: It wants a code from the app.
note: Devices “want” things. Very common and slightly funny.

text: Mình dùng bản miễn phí.
sample: I'm on the free plan.
note: “On” for subscription tiers. Free plan, basic plan, pro plan.

text: Mình mới học dùng cái này.
sample: I've only just started using it.
note: “Only just” = very recently. Extremely common construction.

text: Mình để máy chạy qua đêm.
sample: I left it running overnight.
note: Leave + -ing for a continuing state. Precise and natural.

text: Điện thoại mình nóng quá.
sample: My phone's getting really hot.
note: Get + adjective for change of state. Devices, weather, people.

text: Mình chuyển sang dùng máy tính bảng.
sample: I've switched to using a tablet for that.
note: Switch to = change habits or tools. Very high-frequency.

text: Mình không muốn chia sẻ vị trí.
sample: I'd rather not share my location.
note: The politest possible refusal. Works for anything.

text: Your laptop dies mid-presentation. Handle it out loud in three sentences.
sample: Well — that's the laptop gone. Give me thirty seconds and I'll carry on from memory. It was the good half anyway.
note: Names the disaster calmly and keeps going. The room relaxes.

text: Help a parent over the phone who cannot find an app. Three sentences.
sample: Don't worry, we'll find it. Swipe down from the top and type the first three letters — no, just three. There it is?
note: Short corrective interjections are what real phone support sounds like.

text: Report a bug to a developer clearly, in three sentences.
sample: When I upload a file over ten megabytes, it spins for a minute and then throws a 500. Happens every time on Chrome, not on Safari. I've got the console log if that helps.
note: Trigger, scope, evidence. The three things any developer needs.

text: Explain to a non-technical colleague why the site is down.
sample: One of the servers stopped talking to the database. Nothing is lost — it just can't reach it right now. Half an hour, and I'll message you the moment it's back.
note: Plain-language cause with no jargon. Reassurance first.

text: Ask a shop to fix or replace a phone that broke after two weeks.
sample: I bought it two weeks ago and the screen's already failing — that's not wear and tear. I'd like it replaced rather than repaired, if that's possible.
note: Uses the exact phrase that shifts the argument in your favour.

text: Persuade a friend to back up their files, in two sentences.
sample: You've got one copy of every photo you own, and that copy is in your bag on a bus. Give me ten minutes and I'll set it up for you.
chunk: one copy of every ___ you own
note: Makes an abstract risk vivid. Far better than a lecture.

text: A video call keeps breaking up. Sort it out in the moment.
sample: You're breaking up a bit — shall I turn my camera off and see if that helps?
note: Names the problem and proposes the standard fix in one line.

text: Explain your job to a relative who thinks you fix printers. Three sentences.
sample: I don't fix computers, I write the instructions computers follow. Closer to writing very pedantic recipes than mending anything. And no, I can't get your printer to work either.
note: A fresh analogy plus a joke. Ends the misunderstanding warmly.

text: Ask a colleague to stop sending screenshots and send the actual error text.
sample: Could you paste the error as text rather than a screenshot? I can search text, and I can't search a picture.
note: Gives the reason, which is what makes people actually change.

text: Talk a friend out of buying the newest phone, in three sentences.
sample: Yours is two years old and works perfectly. The new one is the same phone with a better camera you'll use twice. Buy it next year when it's half the price.
note: Reduces the upgrade to its actual difference. Very persuasive.

text: Your account has been locked and support is unhelpful. Escalate in writing.
sample: I've been locked out for four days across three tickets, with no resolution. I'd like this passed to someone who can unlock it today. If that isn't possible, please tell me who can.
note: Firm, specific escalation. Leaves them one obvious action.

text: Teach someone the one habit that will save them the most trouble.
sample: Turn on automatic updates and never think about it again. Ninety percent of the horror stories I hear start with someone clicking 'later' for a year.
note: Advice justified by consequence. Concrete and memorable.

text: Describe a bug that took you three days to find, in three sentences.
sample: Everything worked locally and nothing worked in production. Three days later I found it: a trailing space in a config file. I have never felt so stupid and so relieved at once.
note: The ending makes it a story rather than a report.

text: Politely refuse to be your family’s unpaid IT support, in two sentences.
sample: I'll always help with the important stuff, genuinely. But I'm not the right person for the TV remote — that one's Google's job.
note: Draws the line with a joke. Nobody is offended.

text: Explain to a client why the quick fix is a bad idea, in three sentences.
sample: We can do it by Friday if we hard-code it, and it'll break the first time the data changes. Two extra days buys you something that doesn't need revisiting. Your call, but I'd take the two days.
note: States both options, recommends one, leaves the decision with them.

text: Cuối tuần này bạn rảnh không?
sample: Are you around this weekend?
note: Around = available and nearby. Softer than “are you free”.

text: Thứ Năm bạn thế nào?
sample: How are you fixed for Thursday?
note: Asks about availability idiomatically. Sounds very native.

text: Mình hẹn bảy giờ nhé.
sample: Shall we say seven?
note: Proposes a time gently. The most useful phrase in this whole mood.

text: Mình đến muộn mười phút nhé.
sample: I'm going to be ten minutes behind.
note: Behind = late. Less apologetic than “late”, and more precise.

text: Mình đang trên đường.
sample: I'm on my way.
note: Four words that buy you fifteen minutes of goodwill.

text: Mình phải huỷ hẹn mất.
sample: I'm going to have to cancel, I'm afraid.
note: Distances you from the decision. Softens any cancellation.

text: Mình đổi sang tuần sau được không?
sample: Could we push it to next week?
note: Push = move later. The standard rescheduling verb.

text: Mình muốn dời sớm hơn một tiếng.
sample: Any chance we could bring it forward an hour?
note: Bring forward = make earlier. The opposite of push back.

text: Mình chưa chắc, để mình xem lại.
sample: Let me check and come back to you.
note: Buys time without committing. Completely standard.

text: Mình chốt luôn nhé.
sample: Let's lock it in.
note: Confirms a plan decisively. Modern and very common.

text: Mình đã hẹn chỗ khác rồi.
sample: I've already got something on that night.
note: Vague but complete. Nobody ever asks what.

text: Mình rảnh sau bốn giờ.
sample: I'm free from four onwards.
note: Gives an open window. Easier to schedule against.

text: Bạn chọn giờ nào cũng được.
sample: Any time that suits you works for me.
note: Suit = be convenient for. Very high-frequency verb here.

text: Mình đặt chỗ rồi nhé.
sample: I've booked us a table for eight.
note: “Us” makes it warm and inclusive. Small word, big difference.

text: Mai mình có hẹn cả ngày.
sample: Tomorrow's pretty much wall to wall.

text: Mình sẽ nhắc bạn trước một hôm.
sample: I'll give you a nudge the day before.
note: Gentle reminder. Far friendlier than “I will remind you”.

text: Hẹn gặp lại tuần sau nhé.
sample: See you next week, then.
note: The “then” confirms the plan. Do not drop it.

text: Mình không đi được, xin lỗi nhé.
sample: I can't make it, sorry.
note: Make it = attend. Never “I cannot join”.

text: Mình đến sớm mười lăm phút.
sample: I'll get there a bit early.
note: “A bit” keeps it casual. Being precise sounds anxious.

text: Bạn cứ nhắn khi nào đến nhé.
sample: Text me when you get there.
note: Present simple after “when” for the future. Common error point.

text: Mình chưa có kế hoạch gì.
sample: I've got nothing on, actually.
note: Completely free. The opposite of “something on”.

text: Để mình xem lịch đã.
sample: Let me have a look at my diary.
note: British for calendar. Americans say schedule or calendar.

text: Mình quên mất buổi hẹn.
sample: It completely slipped my mind.
note: Blames memory, not character. The best apology for forgetting.

text: Hôm đó mình không tiện.
sample: That day's a bit awkward for me.
note: Declines a specific date without any reason. Very British.

text: Bọn mình gặp ở đâu nhỉ?
sample: Whereabouts shall we meet?
note: One word for “where roughly”. Sounds properly native.

text: Mình sẽ xác nhận lại sáng mai.
sample: I'll confirm in the morning.
note: Promises a decision with a deadline. Professional and clear.

text: Kế hoạch thay đổi rồi.
sample: There's been a change of plan.
note: Singular “plan” in this fixed phrase. Not “plans”.

text: Mình đi cùng bạn nhé.
sample: I'll come with you, if that's alright.
chunk: I'll come with you, if that's alright
note: Asks permission after stating the intention. Polite and easy.

text: Mình chỉ ở được một tiếng.
sample: I can only stay for an hour, unfortunately.
note: Sets the limit in advance. Prevents an awkward exit.

text: Mình hoãn vô thời hạn.
sample: We've put it off indefinitely.
note: Postponed with no new date. The honest version.

text: Mình sẽ đến nếu tan làm sớm.
sample: I'll come if I can get away early.
note: Get away = leave work. Extremely useful phrasal verb.

text: Bọn mình gặp nhau hằng tháng.
sample: We try to meet up once a month.
note: Meet up = get together socially. The “up” is essential.

text: Mình dự định đi vào tháng Tư.
sample: I'm planning on going in April.
note: Plan on + gerund. Slightly more casual than “plan to”.

text: Bạn rảnh lúc nào thì bảo mình.
sample: Just say when and I’ll work around it.
note: Total flexibility offered in five words. Very generous-sounding.

text: Thôi để lần sau.
sample: Let's do it another time.
note: Keeps the door open without setting a date.

text: Organise dinner with four busy friends over text. Three sentences.
sample: Right — dinner, next Thursday or the Saturday after. Reply with which works and I'll book whatever wins. Silence counts as a yes to both.
note: Two options plus a default. The only method that actually works.

text: Cancel on a close friend two hours before, honestly.
sample: I'm going to be that person and cancel — I'm completely wiped and I'd be terrible company. Can I make it up to you next week? My treat.
chunk: I'm going to be that person
note: Self-aware honesty disarms the annoyance completely.

text: Reschedule a work meeting you double-booked, without admitting the real reason.
sample: Something's come up on my side for Wednesday — could we move it to Thursday morning? Any time before eleven works.
note: The universal blameless excuse. Nobody ever questions it.

text: Turn down an invitation you genuinely do not want to attend.
sample: That's really kind of you to think of me, but I'm going to sit this one out. Have a brilliant time, and send pictures.
chunk: I'm going to sit this one out
note: Declines warmly and closes with enthusiasm for them.

text: Confirm a plan someone made vaguely a week ago, in two sentences.
sample: Just checking we're still on for Friday — seven at the noodle place? Happy either way, just don't want to leave you standing outside.
note: The confirmation everyone forgets to send. Extremely useful.

text: Propose a first meeting with a new contact, giving real options.
sample: Would a coffee work sometime next week? I'm free Tuesday afternoon or Thursday morning — or I can fit around you if neither suits.
chunk: or I can fit around you
note: Two concrete options plus flexibility. Very hard to refuse.

text: You are running badly late and the other person is waiting. Message them.
sample: I'm so sorry — I'm fifteen minutes out. Order something and put it on my tab, I'll be there shortly.
note: Precise time, a solution, and no excuses. The perfect late text.

text: Politely chase someone who has not replied about a date for two weeks.
sample: No pressure at all, just bumping this up your inbox. Still keen whenever you've got a free evening.
note: Light, self-aware nudge. Nobody minds receiving it.

text: Plan a weekend trip with someone indecisive. Take charge in three sentences.
sample: I'm going to book the Saturday train and the place by the lake. If you want to change anything, tell me by Thursday and I'll sort it. Otherwise, bring walking shoes.
chunk: tell me by ___ and I'll sort it
note: Decides, then gives a clear window to object.

text: Someone suggests a time that does not work. Counter-offer without a flat no.
sample: Six is tight for me — could we do half seven instead? Or the same time on Thursday, if that's easier.
note: Never decline without offering an alternative. Keeps momentum.

text: Make a plan with someone in a different time zone.
sample: I'm seven hours ahead of you, so your morning is my evening. Would nine your time work? That's four for me, which is fine.
note: Does their arithmetic for them. Enormously appreciated.

text: A friend keeps making vague plans that never happen. Pin them down kindly.
sample: We've said 'soon' about six times now, which is my fault as much as yours. Pick a date, any date, and I'll put it in ink.
note: Shares the blame, then demands a commitment. Warm and effective.

text: Apologise for missing something important, in three sentences.
sample: I missed it, and there's no good excuse — I had the wrong week in my head. I'm genuinely sorry, especially knowing how much work you put in. Let me hear all about it over lunch, on me.
note: Skipping the excuse is what makes the apology land.

text: End a long planning conversation by summarising the decisions.
sample: So: Saturday the 14th, seven o'clock, I'll book, you bring Linh. Anything I've got wrong?
note: Recap plus an invitation to correct. Prevents every mix-up.
